clue.text: Shelley records his "sneer of cold command"

definitions.text: Shelley records his "sneer of cold command"

parts.words: Shelley records his "sneer of cold command"
parts.note: Shelley's sonnet describes a broken statue of an Egyptian king whose face keeps a 'sneer of cold command'; the clue asks for that king's name

explanation.surface: A note on how a Romantic poet captured a tyrant's haughty look.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'sneer of cold command' comes from Shelley's sonnet about the shattered statue of the pharaoh Rameses II, whom the Greeks called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The sonnet is titled with the Greek name of the pharaoh whose statue wears that sneer.

clue.text: While the water — sings " (John Dyer)

parts.note: a fill-in quotation: the missing word completes a line from John Dyer's poem Grongar Hill

explanation.surface: A gap left in a line of eighteenth-century verse for the solver to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Dyer's Grongar Hill reads 'While the wanton Zephyr sings, / And in the vale perfumes his wings'; the printed 'water' is a misreading of 'wanton'. The missing word is the west wind personified.
explanation.definitionFit: Dyer's line names the gentle west wind, personified as a god, singing over the vale.

clue.text: Monty had a part in his victory

definitions.text: Monty had a part in his victory

parts.words: Monty had a part in his victory
parts.note: turns round the title of a comic war memoir, 'Monty: His Part in My Victory', so 'his' means the memoir's author

explanation.surface: A remark that Field Marshal Montgomery helped some soldier win the war.
explanation.walkthrough: Spike Milligan's war memoirs include 'Monty: His Part in My Victory'; the clue restates the title from the outside, so 'his' is the comedian who wrote it.
explanation.definitionFit: The comedian Spike Milligan wrote the memoir crediting Montgomery with a part in his own wartime victory.

clue.text: Rembrandt's security men

definitions.meaning: Rembrandt's most famous group portrait of a militia company is known by this title
guards patrolling after dark, keeping watch over a town or building

explanation.surface: Asking who guarded the Dutch master's studio.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt's militia painting has this popular title, and guards on duty after dark form such a watch.

clue.text: It will ever be the same, said Smart in the Hilliad

definitions.text: It will ever be the same, said Smart in the Hilliad

parts.words: It will ever be the same, said Smart in the Hilliad
parts.note: Christopher Smart's mock-heroic poem The Hilliad, an attack on the hack John Hill, says that empty foolishness never changes

explanation.surface: A line about unchanging things quoted from an eighteenth-century satirical poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Smart wrote The Hilliad to mock the writer John Hill; the clue's 'It' stands for the quality the poem says will always be the same: emptiness of mind.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality Smart's satire pins on Hill is silly emptiness, which the poem says never changes.

clue.text: Writer for whom Peter øeg's physicist had a feeling

definitions.meaning: C P ..., the British novelist and physicist who wrote Strangers and Brothers

definitions.text: for whom Peter øeg's physicist had a feeling
definitions.meaning: Peter Høeg's novel is Miss Smilla's Feeling for ..., whose heroine studies ice

explanation.surface: A Danish novel's scientist fancies some author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for whom' makes the writer sound like a person, but the second sense is the frozen stuff in the title of Høeg's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: C P Snow was an English novelist, and Høeg's heroine Smilla has a feeling for frozen flakes of ice in the title.

clue.text: Rascal is revealed by her letters

indicators.note: the rascal's true form is brought out by rearranging the clue's letters, so these words signal a reshuffle

explanation.surface: A scoundrel is exposed through a woman's correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revealed by' rearranges RASCAL IS. Richardson's novel is told in its heroine's letters, and its rascal, Lovelace, is indeed exposed by them.
explanation.definitionFit: Richardson's epistolary novel is made up almost wholly of its heroine's correspondence, so it is her letters.

clue.text: Ornament of the church sounds impolite on panel

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second
says the next word is taken by how it is pronounced, not how it is written

parts.note: impolite means rude
a panel used as a partition is a screen

explanation.surface: A church furnishing seems rude when placed on a board.
explanation.walkthrough: A rood is a crucifix; the carved partition carrying it separates nave from chancel.
explanation.definitionFit: The carved partition between nave and chancel carries a crucifix and is a decorative feature of many churches.

clue.text: O'Neill confused by ornamental metalwork

indicators.note: the playwright's name is jumbled, which signals its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The playwright O'Neill baffled by fancy metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' rearranges O'NEILL; the apostrophe gives no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a black metallic inlay used to decorate engraved silver or gold.

clue.text: The cardinal's was his for life

definitions.text: The cardinal's was his for life

parts.words: The cardinal's was his for life
parts.note: Cardinal Newman's autobiography is titled with the Latin 'pro vita sua', for his life, so the clue translates that title

explanation.surface: A churchman's lifelong possession.
explanation.walkthrough: Newman's Apologia Pro Vita Sua means 'a defence of his own life'; 'for life' reads like 'lifelong' but translates 'pro vita sua'.
explanation.definitionFit: Newman's defence of his religious life is a formal written justification of his own views.

clue.text: Provenance of Dvorak's Fifth

parts.note: Dvořák's symphony 'From the ...' was first published as his Fifth, now numbered Ninth, so its title gives where it came from

explanation.surface: Asking where a Czech composer's symphony originated.
explanation.walkthrough: The symphony now called No 9 was published as No 5; its subtitle 'From the New World' names America, where Dvořák wrote it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dvořák wrote the symphony in America, and its subtitle names the Americas as where it comes from.

clue.text: One of Aristophanes' old jumpers

parts.note: Aristophanes wrote a comedy whose chorus are leaping amphibians; 'jumpers' can also sound like knitted pullovers

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek dramatist's worn-out pullover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumpers' suggests sweaters (British for pullovers), but here it means leaping creatures, the croaking chorus of Aristophanes' comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristophanes' comedy has a chorus of croaking amphibians, each a leaping creature.

clue.text: Shakespearean king might be a firstborn …

indicators.note: says the following letters could become something else if rearranged

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean monarch might be the eldest child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' rearranges A FIRSTBORN. The Norwegian prince takes Denmark's throne at the end of Hamlet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norwegian prince in Hamlet claims the Danish crown at the end, becoming king.

clue.text: Accompaniment to royal progress warms cutie, anyhow

indicators.note: means in any old way, so the letters are put in any order

explanation.surface: Something warms a sweetheart, in a slapdash way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' rearranges WARMS CUTIE. Handel's suite was written for George I's procession on the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: Handel composed the suite to play during King George I's barge procession on the Thames.

clue.text: … and wonder in English poetry seen by Swinburne's supporter as reborn

definitions.text: … and wonder in English poetry seen by Swinburne's supporter as reborn

parts.words: … and wonder in English poetry seen by Swinburne's supporter as reborn
parts.note: Theodore Watts-Dunton, who looked after Swinburne, coined a phrase for Romantic poetry's revival of wonder, describing it as reborn

explanation.surface: A critic says English verse recovered its sense of wonder.
explanation.walkthrough: Watts-Dunton, Swinburne's friend and carer, called the Romantic movement 'the Renascence of Wonder'; the clue asks for the first word of that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Watts-Dunton's phrase names the rebirth of wonder in English poetry, a revival.

clue.text: "In pieces cut, the viper still did —" (Swift)

definitions.text: "In pieces cut, the viper still did —" (Swift)

parts.words: "In pieces cut, the viper still did —" (Swift)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Swift: the missing verb says the cut-up viper's pieces joined together again

explanation.surface: A gap in a line of Swift about a snake that survives being chopped up.
explanation.walkthrough: The old belief was that a severed viper could rejoin its pieces; Swift's line ends on the verb for that.
explanation.definitionFit: The chopped viper's pieces were believed to join back together, coming together again.

clue.text: Tune died sadly, and not changed

indicators.note: the melody dies in an unhappy way, and that unhappiness signals its letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A melody faded sadly away and stayed the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges TUNE DIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Text that has not been revised or altered by an editor is as it was.

clue.text: Beckett's last plays? …

definitions.meaning: Samuel Beckett wrote a one-act play with this title
the closing stage of a game, especially chess, when few pieces remain

explanation.surface: Asking whether these were Beckett's final dramas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plays' reads as dramas, but in the second sense it means moves in a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's play has this title, and a chess game's final stage of moves goes by it.

clue.text: Lively chap in spirited dance

definitions.meaning: an old word for a gay, high-spirited man
a lively Renaissance court dance in triple time

explanation.surface: A jolly fellow taking part in a vigorous dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The word once meant a merry fellow and also names a brisk sixteenth-century court dance.

clue.text: Devious movers from Dallas

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held is 'Devious movers from Dallas' (7): 'Devious movers' fits chess pieces that move crookedly, but nothing found explains 'from Dallas'; possibly an OCR misreading that a search of the text did not resolve.

clue.text: … and spoken words he poisoned, sadly

indicators.note: a poisoning is a sorry business, and that unhappiness signals the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A grim story told aloud of a man who poisoned someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges HE POISONED. The leading dots tie this to the previous clue's chess game.
explanation.definitionFit: Linguists use the term for vivid words that evoke a sound or sensation, words heard in speech.

clue.text: Like Alasdair Gray's spare stories

parts.note: Alasdair Gray shared the collection ... Tales with James Kelman and Agnes Owens; 'spare' also means thin

explanation.surface: A description of a Scottish writer's sparse tales.
explanation.walkthrough: Lean Tales (1985) was a joint story collection by Alasdair Gray, James Kelman and Agnes Owens; 'spare' gives the same adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Gray's joint collection describes the stories as thin and spare.

clue.text: Some Spenserian enamel on the French armour

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: the French au can mean 'on the' or 'at the'
mail is flexible armour of linked rings

explanation.surface: Glazed decoration on a French suit of armour.
explanation.walkthrough: Spenser uses this archaic word for enamel in The Faerie Queene.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser's archaic word means enamelled decoration, the kind applied to metal.

clue.text: He saw it through

parts.note: H G Wells's wartime novel is titled Mr ... Sees It Through, so the clue gives its hero

explanation.surface: Praise for someone who persevered to the end.
explanation.walkthrough: H G Wells's 1916 novel 'Mr Britling Sees It Through' follows an Englishman through the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells's title character is the man who sees the war through.

clue.text: Russian prince with no right to stiffness

indicators.note: says a letter is taken away from the following word

parts.note: rigor is stiffness, as in rigor mortis

explanation.surface: A Russian nobleman without any claim to firmness.
explanation.walkthrough: Borodin's opera Prince Igor is about the prince.
explanation.definitionFit: Borodin's opera is named after the twelfth-century prince of Novgorod-Seversky.

clue.text: Australian novelist's dynasty leads and follows artist

indicators.note: the same piece stands both before and after the middle piece

parts.note: the Han dynasty ruled China
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword's usual artist
the Han dynasty ruled China

explanation.surface: A novelist from Australia comes of a famous family line.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is'. Barbara Hanrahan was an Australian novelist and printmaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbara Hanrahan was a South Australian writer of novels and also a printmaker.

clue.text: Where Othello stabbed a malignant Turk

definitions.text: Where Othello stabbed a malignant Turk

parts.words: Where Othello stabbed a malignant Turk
parts.note: in his final speech Othello recalls killing 'a malignant and a turban'd Turk' in a Syrian city

explanation.surface: Asking the scene of a murder recalled by Shakespeare's Moor.
explanation.walkthrough: Othello's last speech begins the story 'in Aleppo once', naming the Syrian city where he struck the Turk.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello names the Syrian city where he struck down the Turk.

clue.text: "The finest Elphberg of them all"

parts.note: in The Prisoner of Zenda the Elphbergs are Ruritania's royal house, and the English hero who looks like one is praised as the best of them

explanation.surface: Praise for the best member of a royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: In Anthony Hope's The Prisoner of Zenda, Rudolf, an English gentleman with the Elphberg red hair, stands in for the king and proves nobler than any true Elphberg.
explanation.definitionFit: Hope's hero, an Englishman descended from the Ruritanian royals, is called the finest of that line.
